options.label: Draw on the HELOC
options.note: Enough today, and worse than it looks. $1,067.84 of a $202,654 limit, 99.5% drawn, at 4.90% interest-only, so the draw never amortises — and because the interest capitalises rather than being paid, a $623 draw becomes a permanent addition to the balance, not a debt that clears. $2,269.80 of past lacrosse fees already went on it this way. The decisive point is the timing: the HELOC capitalises about $814 a month with nothing repaying it, so it passes its own limit on 30 September WITHOUT anyone borrowing another dollar. Drawing $623 for the registrations brings that to 31 August — about three weeks away — and leaves $444.84 of headroom against a monthly charge of $814. This is not a source of funds, it is a source of an over-limit breach on the household's largest revolving facility.

budget.note: What the weekly household cap has to cover, category by category. Amounts are NOT stored here — they are derived at render time from public/periods.json, the generated spending history, so there is one home for every historical figure. This block carries only the classification (essential, discretionary, reserve, unknown), which dated bills and commitments belong to each category, and any owner target that should beat the historical average.
budget.classNote: ESSENTIAL is normal life with no reliable date — groceries, fuel, phones. It comes out of the weekly cap first. DISCRETIONARY is reducible. RESERVE is a real cost that does not fall inside this 90-day window and must be saved for rather than spent. DATED bills and commitments are already on the calendar as events and are subtracted from their category so nothing is paid twice.

ownerTargets.note: Nine owner budget targets are now incorporated, supplied directly by the owner on 2026-08-10 and recorded here with that provenance. They are NOT workbook-verified: monthly_budget_tracker_template.xlsx and HOME BUDGET.xlsx are still absent from this repository and from the machine this ran on, so three things remain unconfirmed - (1) that these nine are current and complete rather than a subset, (2) the AMOUNTS of the sinking funds, which were named but not quantified, and (3) whether the owner's 'Personal' line maps to the transaction record's Shopping category. Every category without a target below is still a historical actual and is labelled as one.
ownerTargets.sinkingFundsNote: Named by the owner but NOT quantified, so no amount is modelled for them. Property tax and CRA are carried as reserves from the historical record; the Fusion and Burrard commitments are dated on the calendar with owner-stated amounts. Home insurance, Christmas, travel, annual bills and the emergency top-up have no figure and are OWNER DECISION REQUIRED - the workbook would supply them.

budget.cardCaveat: The historical averages below are total household spending — chequing, cards and PayPal. The forecast deducts the weekly cap as CASH from the household chequing accounts, but only card MINIMUMS as debt service. Spending at the historical rate on the cards would therefore show a healthy cash line while the card balances grew. The cap is a cash instruction, and it only holds if the spending is actually paid for rather than carried.

nextDollar.provenanceNote: DERIVED PLAN POLICY, not an owner instruction. Neither Dale nor Amanda has stated or approved this ordering; it was derived by the implementation from the current financial facts — the penalty-rate clock on the TD credit card, the over-limit fee on the Cash Back Visa, and the HELOC crossing its own limit inside the window. It was previously presented as a household decision, which no owner statement supported. The ordering is offered as a recommendation and remains open to the owner overriding it; if they adopt it, this would change this field to owner-stated with a dated reference.
nextDollar.summary: The next surplus dollar goes to the TD Cash Back Visa: it is the highest rate the household pays at 26.99%, and it is the only card currently over its limit, so paying it down removes an interest charge and a monthly over-limit fee at the same time.

order.why: Every dated minimum and the mortgage come first. A missed minimum on the TD credit card is the most expensive event available to this household — a fifth one restarts the 24.99% penalty rate for another twelve months.
The 12 August registrations cannot clear on $79.84. Nothing else in the plan matters until they can.

The TD Cash Back Visa is $612.43 over its $5,000 limit and is charged a $29 monthly over-limit fee on top of 26.99% interest. Getting it back inside the limit is a guaranteed return, not a forecast one.
Below that, an ordinary mistimed bill becomes an NSF fee and an overdraft charge, which is how the last twelve months produced $145/month of avoidable bank fees.
Groceries, fuel, phones and medical. Cutting these to service debt is how a plan gets abandoned in week three.

order.rule: Stop new HELOC and revolving growth
order.why: The HELOC capitalises about $814 a month with nothing repaying it, and passes its own limit inside this window on that alone. Any new draw brings that date forward. This ranks above extra repayment because growth compounds against every future month.

order.rule: Direct verified surplus to the highest effective-cost consumer debt
order.why: By rate that is the TD Cash Back Visa at 26.99%, then the TD credit card at its 24.99% penalty rate, then Triangle at 21.99%. Effective cost, not headline rate: the Cash Back card also carries the over-limit fee, which makes its real cost higher still.

nextDollar.note: Encoded explicitly so the plan cannot quietly apply a different one, and evaluated against current facts rather than applied blindly: the ordering puts stopping HELOC growth above extra card repayment specifically because the HELOC breaches its limit inside this window without anyone borrowing another dollar. See provenanceNote — this is Atlas's recommendation, not a household decision.

assumptions: The window is the 13 weeks (91 days) starting on the as-of date. Every date in the projection is derived from that date — nothing is hardcoded to a calendar month.
Deposits are assumed to land before payments due the same day. Payday-timed bills (the mortgage on the 14th) are arranged on exactly that assumption.
Every figure is tagged. Confirmed means the institution or a long observed history states it; estimated means it is modelled and shown in amber with a ≈ mark throughout.
Future card statement minimums are estimates carried at the current level; real minimums move with the balance.

Named recurring bills — FortisBC, Shaw, BCAA, ICBC, the children's RESP contribution, CMAW Local 1995 union dues, Fit4Less, the TD account fees — are dated on the calendar with days extracted from the transaction history or, for the RESP, from the owner-stated hard bill, and are excluded from the variable budget so nothing is counted twice. The RESP is an internal transfer, not a spending category. Union dues remain dated until cancellation is actually confirmed; the cancel action stays open and the bill is retired when evidence closes it. The 1 September BC Hydro $237.45 due is a household obligation paid from Amanda / DEBT&PAYMENTS: it is dated, it does not reduce joint cash, and it is not subtracted from household averages. The variable budget covers everything else: groceries, fuel, phones, streaming, PayPal and the rest.

One known cost has no reliable date and is NOT on the calendar: the Telus phone bills, absent from every captured account since March 2026, route unknown. It rides inside the household budget's telecom average instead. The $213.79 Hydro amount that was due 14 August is also not dated here — later settlement status is unknown (Q17).

Each week's 'keep above' figure is the closing balance below which the rest of the window would breach the buffer even with everything going to plan — it is the week-by-week track to stay on, computed backwards from the end of the window.

The plan is the HOUSEHOLD SPENDING ACCOUNTS ONLY — Chequing A, Chequing B and Savings. Amanda's DEBT&PAYMENTS account is a separate pot: her Tennis BC pay lands there, coaches are paid from it, and only the remainder crosses over. Neither its balance nor her gross pay is counted as household money; only her actual transfers are, measured from the transfer record. Internal transfers between household accounts are excluded throughout.

Because her account is excluded, so is most of what it pays. She settles BC Hydro, part of the MBNA minimum and some card payments direct from it — roughly $940/month that does not reduce joint cash. The 1 September Hydro $237.45 due is dated as an external household obligation for that reason. Every card minimum is nonetheless charged to the household here, which is the cautious reading: if she keeps paying a share, the household finishes better than shown.

HELOC interest is capitalised, not paid. It is charged as a debit on the HELOC itself at month-end and no matching chequing payment exists, so it is shown on the calendar and excluded from the cash maths. That is not good news — it means the balance grows by about $814 every month with nothing repaying it.
No bonus is modelled: bonuses have historically landed in February and July, outside this window.
The recommended weekly budget is solved from the forecast: the largest weekly spend that keeps the projected balance above the target buffer on every single day of the window.

Room for extra debt repayment is measured at the end of the window — cash projected above the buffer once every obligation and commitment has cleared. Paying it earlier than the low point would breach the buffer.

The HELOC passes its own limit inside this window with no new borrowing. It is 99.5% drawn, its interest capitalises onto the balance at about $814 a month, and nothing repays it — so the balance crosses $202,654 on 30 September on that alone. This is projected from the observed charge, not read from a statement, and it is why stopping HELOC growth ranks above extra card repayment in the next-dollar policy.

Loan-to-value on the mortgage and HELOC together ($747,612.74) is 68% at the low end and 53% at the high end, both comfortably under the 80% that matters at the May 2027 renewal. This is an owner's estimate, not an appraisal, and a lender will use its own. Vehicles, pensions and the business are still excluded.

interestCheck.note: The $158.55 is explained, and the question was mis-specified rather than unanswerable. Two things were wrong with the expected "about $115". It applied 26.99% to the CLOSING balance, but interest is charged on the average daily balance — on a card paid down and run back up those are different numbers. And it looked at August alone: June and July were charged below rate, at an effective 21.98% and 17.69%, leaving $45.46 uncollected; August then ran at 36.46% and collected it. Across five cycles the model implies $504.37 against $492.64 actually charged — a 2.3% gap, which is the transaction-date-versus-posting-date bias and nothing more.
interestCheck.cash: The cash-advance theory is dead on the statements' own evidence: every interest line on this card, in all twelve statements, is headed RETAIL INTEREST. There is no cash-advance bucket, so the 27.99% rate was never part of it.

counterparties.note: TD's export never names the other side of an e-transfer — outgoing reads SEND E-TFR ***GCa and nothing more. Interac's confirmation emails do name them, and sweeping both mailboxes properly took attribution from 24 of 204 to 49 — it has doubled. Every one of the 26 newly recovered transfers matches a bank row on amount and date, so this is corroboration, not guesswork.
counterparties.finding: Almost every newly recovered notification was in the bin. Gmail purges deleted mail after 30 days, so the counterparty record is being destroyed on a rolling 30-day cycle — which is the real reason coverage looked hopeless, and why it will stay poor unless something changes. It also means the previous conclusion was wrong: the notifications were not missing, they were deleted.
counterparties.action: A Gmail filter on both accounts that labels and archives mail from payments.interac.ca instead of deleting it costs nothing and makes every future transfer attributable. It cannot recover what has already been purged — everything deleted before roughly 10 July 2026 is gone.
counterparties.matching: The matcher was also wrong: it named every transfer of the same amount within four days from a single notification, and would let an incoming notification name an outgoing transfer. It now matches one notification to one transfer, nearest date first, direction enforced.

questions.q: What does the coaching business actually net?
questions.detail: There are TWO businesses and the question has been conflating them. Amanda's coaching business takes in large e-transfers — 8 of over $3,000 totalling $42,395 — but she pays her coaches out of that, so it is revenue, not income. Her parents' dental lab is the other, run from the garage, which paid $1,000–1,100/month of rent until it stopped in May 2026. Coach payments cannot be separated from personal transfers in the bank data.
questions.changes: Household income is currently overstated by up to $1,650/month. Every conclusion resting on income is provisional until this is split. Amanda's bookkeeping settles it.

questions.q: Where do the coach payments leave from?
questions.detail: One coach is paid by cheque from DEBT&PAYMENTS — five cheques, $8,150, February to November 2025. But they stop in November 2025 while her sheets show $6,397.50 of coach pay between April and August 2026. Meanwhile the 30 June remittance of $9,646.25 went onto the HELOC the same day it arrived.
questions.changes: Whether pass-through money owed to coaches was spent on household debt. Also points at the account outside the captured set — the same one that may be one of the two unidentified accounts.

questions.q: Is the garage rent coming back, and what does a lab in the garage mean?
questions.detail: Her parents moved their dental lab into the garage and paid $1,000–1,100/month until May 2026, when it stopped because that business is not going well. This was misfiled for 18 months as a spousal transfer rather than rental income on the home.
questions.changes: $12,600/year of income that disappeared without registering as an income event. Business use of the home may also affect insurance, and creates both a possible deduction and a capital-gains exposure worth an accountant's view before the May 2027 renewal.

questions.q: Where does the rest of the $19,700 of e-transfers go?
questions.detail: $3,500 is now traced to the Wise holiday accounts. The remainder still leaves the household without a matched destination, $13,062 of it originally drawn from the HELOC.
questions.changes: The working theory is business inventory. If so it is a business cost currently counted as household spending, and it is being funded by borrowing against the house.

questions.q: What are the two unidentified accounts?
questions.detail: One sent $33,598 across 142 transfers; the other received $16,945 across five.
questions.changes: $59,027 of movement, likely folding into question 1.

questions.q: Why did the wife's monthly transfer stop after May 2026?

questions.changes: ~$1,100/month. If the payment method changed, the money may still be arriving elsewhere. If the income changed, the household budget needs rebuilding around it.
